newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich says he won't surrender speaker's post.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich says he won't surrender speaker's post.

text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich, besieged by speculation about his political future, made it plain on Friday that he will remain at the helm of the House of Representatives if Republicans hold on to their majority in November.

While campaigning in his home district in Georgia, the conservative leader said that by bowing to partisan attacks and handing the gavel over to a new Republican speaker he would only give Democrats a new target "to lie about."
"I don't think there's a single person who thinks I'm not going to be speaker, on the Republican side," Gingrich told reporters after speaking to school children at a suburban elementary school.
"You'd just have a new target for the liberals to lie about. Since there's nothing positive left (for them) to say, they'd simply have to create a new false person."

Gingrich, 53, a main architect of the so-called Republican revolution, this week took the rare step of refuting a conservative Boston Globe columnist's report that Gingrich had told fund-raisers he would resign from office rather than face a House ethics investigations in the hands of Democrats.

In a written statement denying the "ridiculous assertion," the speaker said he would only relinquish party leadership in the event of a Democratic victory, but would remain in Congress as an ordinary representative.
But political experts later said Gingrich's role could be diminished even if Republicans retained control of the House.

The former history professor, blamed for two government shutdowns last winter, has come to be seen as a political albatross for many Republican congressional candidates in this year's election campaign because of his widespread unpopularity with voters.
Given that, some experts believe his party colleagues no longer owe him the allegiance they did in 1994, when he led Republicans to their first takeover of Congress in 40 years.
The House race is considered a toss-up. But Gingrich has predicted that Republicans will pick up between 6 and 20 seats in the chamber on Nov. 5.

On Friday, he was more optimistic than usual about the chances of another Republican victory, saying the party is beginning to make headway against what he termed a false national advertising campaign by labour unions and trial lawyers.
"I think gradually we're actually winning the argument around the country, because people are figuring it out," he said.
Gingrich also defended the legislative aims of the Republican revolution, saying they fall right in step with the concerns of the U.S. electorate.
"We're simply reflecting the core vision of the American people," he told reporters, before embarking on a list of Republican goals that included no reference to unpopular Medicare reforms.

"We drew most of the vision out of the American people. It's not our vision. It's the vision of the American people. The American people want a balanced budget. The American people want welfare reform. The American people are tired of drug dealers destroying their children."
